newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-WOODS FACES TEST OF NERVE AT TROON.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-WOODS FACES TEST OF NERVE AT TROON.

text.p: Tiger Woods will face another daunting opponent similar to the one which floored him at last month's U.S. Open when he tackles Royal Troon in the British Open next week.

Golf's astounding new phenomenon will confront a layout not quite as fierce as the Congressional Club turned out to be, but with an equally ferocious reputation if the wind on the west coast of Scotland blows as it can.

After his glorious 12-stroke triumph in the Masters at Augusta in April, there was talk of Woods winning the impossibly difficult 'Grand Slam' of all four major titles in his first year as a professional.
Then Congressional stepped in. "This golf course beat me up. It humbled me big-time," he said after finishing six over par, in joint 19th place and 10 strokes behind winner Ernie Els.
Next week will reveal how much Woods learned from that salutary experience.
It remains to be seen if the length, the narrowness, the rough and the wind at Royal Troon hurt Woods as much as the tight fairways, thick, clingy rough and slippery greens at Congressional did.

Or whether Nick Faldo, Colin Montgomerie, Ernie Els and Greg Norman and the rest of the world's top players with far greater experience of those conditions will prove too tough for him in an alien environment.
Norman emphasised on Thursday that "Tiger has the game to win on any golf course" but two previous trips to Britain do not augur well for his chances.
In 1995 at 19, he was already the U.S. amateur champion, hitting the ball a country mile and having his praises sung lustily throughout the golfing world.
Yet he could only manage joint 47th place in the Scottish Open and joint 66th in the British Open.
Last year, despite a second amateur title, his promise remained unfulfilled when he missed the cut at the Scottish Open before improving to joint 22nd at Royal Lytham in the British Open.
But his decision late last summer to quit university and concentrate on golf full-time as a professional brought about a change in his fortunes almost beyond belief.

He heads golf's world rankings with a haul of seven titles in only 10 months as a pro, already has one Masters green jacket and remains the only player to have won three U.S. junior and three senior amateur titles.

When he turned pro he signed a clothing contract for $40 million with the Nike firm, one of $3.5 million with golf ball makers Titleist and several others which took the total to an estimated $60 million.
Not bad for a black player barely out of his teens in what has been traditionally a white man's sport.
Yet he arrived for his first pro tournament with only $10 in his pocket and had to ask his coach for $100 so he could enter the event.
Woods proved to be a fast learner, tying for 60th then improving to 11th, joint fifth and joint third before winning only his fifth pro tournament, the Las Vegas Invitational.
This year he captured the Mercedes Championship in January and the Asian Masters in Thailand in February before arriving at Augusta in April as the Masters favourite.
That assessment seemed misplaced after an opening four-over-par front nine of 40 shots.
Then he proceeded to tear the famed course apart, compiling a 70 after a back nine of 30 and adding rounds of 66 and 65 to establish a nine-shot lead.
A closing 69 made him the youngest ever Masters champion by a record 12 strokes on 18 under par, achieved without hitting more than a seven-iron approach to any par-four holes on the course.
On a course tailor-made for him with its wide fairways, he drove an average of nearly 330 yards that week, even playing one par-five with a driver and a wedge.

Jack Nicklaus, heralded as the greatest of all time and himself the winner of six green jackets, said of Woods: "He plays a game with which I am not familiar," echoing the words of Bobby Jones about Nicklaus back in 1965.
Since then Woods has added the Byron Nelson Classic in Texas and the Western Open last Sunday as a prelude to his eagerly-awaited British Open challenge.

Woods, who according to his father Earl first picked up a club at the age of nine months, swapping voluntarily from left-handed to right-handed a month later, is adamant he has no problem dealing with the adulation or the expectations of others.
"Others people's expectations have no bearing on what I expect to do. I live not for them, but for me."
A windblown Troon, nevertheless, could stretch Tiger's fortitude to its limits.
